note: An early public sector risk taxonomy with an accountability structure, useful for government clients that predate current AI policy.
title: Administration by algorithm: A risk management framework
explain_beginner: This paper looks at computer systems that make decisions in government services. The authors point out that these systems can carry hidden biases that unfairly affect people or groups, and these problems are hard to spot or prove. The paper offers a simple way to sort these systems into types and a framework for managing the risks, including clear accountability and rules. It matters because governments need a structured way to make sure automated decisions are fair and someone is responsible when things go wrong.
explain_business: For executives serving government clients, this paper signals that automated decision systems carry reputational and legal risks, particularly when bias is embedded and hard to prove, or when work is outsourced. The authors provide a risk management framework with an accountability structure and regulatory governance, which can guide how you design, document, and oversee public sector AI projects. The practical decision is to adopt structured accountability and governance early, rather than waiting for formal AI rules, since this framework predates current policy and can inform compliance planning.
explain_practitioner: The authors propose a taxonomy of public sector decision-making algorithms, noting that algorithmic decisions are not new and are not always AI-based. They argue that risks go beyond errors, since values and biases can become embedded in software and are difficult to detect or prove, especially with poor transparency, weak accountability, or private outsourcing. Using the taxonomy, they build a risk management framework with components including an accountability structure and regulatory governance, intended to support structured accountability and legal regulation of AI in the public sphere.
